#3941. 'Retire Dragon Quest and Make a New RPG': Drama Surrounds Dragon Quest After Mobile Game Reveal

Square Enix criticised for Toriyama credits

I don't think the future of Dragon Quest has ever seemed so murky.

The timeless series finds itself in a bit of a predicament, with Dragon Quest 12 taking forever to come out, and the tragic passing of franchise artist Akira Toriyama only adding to the surrounding uncertainty.

And while the recent remakes have done well to fill the gap, it does feel like fan patience is becoming stretched for the first time in ages.

Case in point: the newly announced Dragon Quest RPG The Cursed Tree and the Chosen Isle — a mobile spin-off set to launch next year — has been met with a surprising amount of frustration.

Japanese social media has been full of disgruntled fans; some have, again, grown annoyed by the series' relative stagnation, while others have voiced their displeasure over Dragon Quest's continued use of Toriyama's unmistakable art style.

One viral post has a pop at the new mobile game's protagonist, simply pointing out that Toriyama would never have drawn a scabbard that doesn't match its sword's length.

In other words, the quality has fallen off without Toriyama — and yet Square Enix is still crediting him as the character designer.

But what's really caused a fuss is a short blog post by veteran video game composer Yasunori Mitsuda, who worked on Chrono Trigger alongside Toriyama.

In the post, Mitsuda offers his own thoughts on the aforementioned drama. He remains respectful, but it's clear that he's got strong feelings on the state of Dragon Quest as a whole.

"I feel that this direction is not good for the artist, Akira Toriyama fans, and even for the late Akira Toriyama himself," Mitsuda explains.

He continues: "As a personal opinion, since it's impossible to create anything truly new no matter how hard you try, I feel that the Dragon Quest series should be brought to an end, and [series creator Yuji Horii] should create a new RPG."

"What's important is that the game provides dreams, hope, and experiences that can only be had through games to the younger generation of children who will play it in the future. But every time I see topics like this, I realise just how wonderful Dragon Quest is and how it has captivated so many people."

So, what are your thoughts on Dragon Quest at this point in time? Are you feeling similar frustrations? Strike down some slimes in the comments section below.

The filmmaker and author of Terrible Old Games You've Probably Never Heard Of gives us a tour of his Steam library.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Welcome to Disk Cleanup, our regular weekend feature delving into the PCs of PC gaming luminaries. Come back every weekend to read a new interview, digging into the important questions, like "How tidy is your desktop?" and "What game will you never uninstall?"

Stuart Ashen—better known by his YouTube persona Ashens—grew up on a diet of 8-bit games on consoles like the Atari 2600 and the Spectrum. The earliest PC game he recalls playing was Syndicate Wars on his first home-built rig—a Pentium 200 MMX machine housed in a server tower case: "I loved Syndicate. Hated Syndicate Wars. Never got on with it at all," he says. "Ended up giving it to a friend who loved it … I think I went on to Duke Nukem 3D or something."

Alongside his video work, Ashens is currently making a folk horror film told in reverse. "Unfortunately, it's far enough away from release that there's no point plugging it," he says. But he hit pause on production to guide me through the haunted arcade of his PC. We talked DOS fighting games, the problem with rangers in RPGs, and the worst retro game Ashens has ever played.

I'm currently playing Gloomhaven, the digital version of the board game, for the second time. I put about 150 hours into it, then sort of left it, and I've come back to it.

It's kind of fantastic. I love board games, but Gloomhaven is one I didn't think I would ever play, because I know it takes two hours to set up or something. When the computer is taking control of all the bits and bobs, you can play it on your own in the background while you're doing other things and waiting for stuff. That’s going to get a lot of time from me.

It's all team-based. It's all your standard band of different [fantasy] archetypes together, and then after they reach a certain level, that's not true. When they do a certain personal quest thing, which can be a pain in the arse for various reasons, they retire, and then you can replace them with other ones you've unlocked. So the team basically changes, and the whole dynamic changes over time, which is something that's really kept me interested.

The previous game would have been Baldur's Gate 3, and it is still installed. I should uninstall it for two reasons. One, it takes up a lot of space, and two, I might start playing it and it will eat all my spare time again. Because, yeah, I got kind of obsessed.

From the creators of Edge: A free weekly videogame industry newsletter, featuring in-depth news, expert analysis and exclusive interviews

To give you an idea, I'm now on 350 hours on Gloomhaven, but 927 on Baldur's Gate. Probably a good 50 to 100 hours of that is just sitting in the background [but] it's so far ahead of any other game I've played in terms of hours, it's unbelievable.

I've never played a Larian game [before], and I didn't like the early Baldur's Gate games. I got the first one free with a graphics card. I remember opening the graphics card box and about 14 discs fell out. I was so excited to play it and I could not get on with the combat. It was that weird, sort of issue commands and pause and do things. It just didn't do anything for me, and I thought, "Oh, that's disappointing." After a couple of hours, I never came back to it.

And then I saw something about Baldur's Gate 3—because I wasn't interested in it at all for obvious reasons, and it just had that spark to it of, "Hang on, there's something special going on here, with the writing of that." And then I saw they changed the combat to turn based, and I was like, "Right, sign me up."

I bought it, installed it, started playing it, and that was the only thing I played probably for two and a half, three years.

This isn't one I played a lot—we have this because we were streaming it. But it's Street Fighter for DOS from 1988.

It's entirely different to the arcade version, I think it's got more in common with the weird Commodore 64 version. But basically, we were going through, on stream, every single DOS fighting game, and it's pretty bad. But weirdly, not as bad as a lot of them.

DOS fighting games are, like, for every good one, there's five really bad ones and one that you can't believe they'd charge money for. It barely works. I love fighting games, so it's always interesting to see these obscure ones we haven't heard of. But God, the DOS ones! It was like they saw Mortal Kombat but absolutely did not understand Mortal Kombat. So you've just got teenagers dancing around in front of a camcorder, badly digitised, and some Christ-awful game engine that just does not work fundamentally.

Then again, the arcade game is awful for the first Street Fighter. There's just not really much of a game to it. Even in the arcade, it's all about learning the special moves and repeating them over and over. Or trying to, because the controls are not quite there for Street Fighter 1. I think that's got to be one of the biggest improvements in history, from Street Fighter 1 to Street Fighter 2.

I think I [initially] did a Ranger. I'm always interested in Rangers in RPGs, because they're never implemented very well. In EverQuest, it was the [class] that could dish a lot of damage and yet couldn't take any. It was just noticeably inferior …. It felt better in Baldur's Gate 3. It probably wasn't the optimal build, but it did actually work. I do like the ranged bow combat, and I'm always interested in why they never get it right. Is it just nobody likes Rangers, but they feel they have to put them in anyway?

I didn't go Dark Urge until the second playthrough, not really understanding what it was at the time, obviously. And then I was informed after, "Oh, you should try that." And I'm like, "Oh, this is what the game was written for. OK, yes, it's even better now."

It's absolutely incredible. Writing, performance, everything is a step above anything that had come before, I think. And the combat is so much fun, which obviously is super important because that's a huge percentage of it.

That is Command & Conquer 3: Kane's Wrath. Because sometimes, if I've got 10 minutes spare, I'll just quickly start up a skirmish map on it, just a simple 1v1, and see how quickly I can win, and that's it. It's almost a comfort thing. I only do it once maybe every couple of months, but I'll always leave it installed for that reason. Plus, by today's standards, it doesn't take up much room.

I think I like the skirmish better in 3, due to the variety of all the bits and bobs in it. It's probably not the tightest of the games in the series. But for me, that's the one I always enjoyed the most.

There's a little window, and you type in the name of any file on your PC, and it's already indexed them, and it instantly appears with where they all are, and you can easily narrow things down. Life changing. The amount of files I've given stupid names to, or put in the wrong folder that I've just found immediately because of this. It's fundamentally changed the way I work.

Oh dear. So I have icons turned off on the desktop. I'm going to turn them back on, if I can remember how.

Fuck! I'm turning that off. Oh no, that's not good. That's pretty bad. Oh God! How do I turn them off? Oh God, it's horrible.

It's just two 4k monitors entirely covered in icons and stuff. Because I don't use the desktop at all, so I just let it auto install things there and forget about it. I've got a little program called RocketDock, which keeps the useful things on the side of one of the monitors, and that's it. I've not looked at the actual desktop in years, and it is monstrous.

One I only briefly played back in the day, and then something made me play it again on stream, and it was so much better than I remembered, [is] Moonstone for the Amiga. It's like a hack 'n' slash-y, brawler type thing, but with a lot of RPG elements. It's also beautifully designed, with really nice artwork and sound. But it's a really interesting game. No other game quite has the vibe of it. Not to say it's the best game ever or anything, but it's still very bloody good.

What is the worst overall? Oh man, there's so many bad ones. There's one called, which we keep talking about [on stream], Graeme Souness Vector Soccer. This isn't the worst. I'm just going to mention it because it's great. It's an Amiga game, and literally the characters are vectors. But of course, due to the way they didn't really have the processing power back then, these vectors look like the Keep Britain Tidy logo. So they're all weird things moving around and the frame rate is monstrous. It's like three frames a second. It's totally unplayable. Nobody seems to know if there's a good game under the hood or not.

I think for absolute worst, it's got to be SQIJ! And it's for the Spectrum. There are versions for other computers that are perfectly competent. But the Spectrum one was written by a man, or a boy at the time, bless him, called Jason Creighton, who really didn't want to fucking write it or work at that company again. So he just spat out something absolutely awful that basically is borderline unplayable, sent it to them, and they just didn't bother looking at it. They just loaded it, went 'Oh, that loads.' Put it on tape, out it goes.

Powerhouse, the company that released it, released it twice—a standard release and then a release later on as a compilation. As released, it doesn't work. Basically, Jason accidentally turned on the caps lock or something in the source code, and you can't turn it off, and the keys actually don't function if caps lock is on. So you load it up and you can't move. That's it. Fortunately, it's so badly put together you can literally break into the program and turn the caps lock off through poking a memory access directly, if you know what I mean. And by the time you've hacked it to work, it's just no fun whatsoever.

The 30th D.I.C.E. awards will feature the presentation of the inaugural award

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The Academy of Interactive Arts and Sciences (AIAS) has confirmed that Mario, Donkey Kong and The Legend of Zelda creator Shigeru Miyamoto will be the inaugural recipient of its new Legend Award.

AIAS – which runs the annual D.I.C.E. Awards – has confirmed that for the 30th edition of its award show it will introduce a new award, that being the Legend Award. This award is being treated as the most exclusive accolade AIAS can give, with it being described as a "generational honor," so much so that it will be presented only once per decade.

It's intended for "an industry icon whose enduring vision continues to redefine interactive entertainment. Honoring creators whose groundbreaking achievements have already earned lasting universal acclaim, this award also celebrates their immeasurable impact and influence that is still being felt in the work of game makers and entertainers in every entertainment medium today and well into our future," it's explained.

Meggan Scavio, president of the AIAS says in a press release, "Shigeru Miyamoto is widely recognized as one of the most respected and impactful figures in the games industry and beyond." She explains, "We believe he perfectly embodies our inaugural Legend Award through his impact and reach, and we are so humbled and excited to have Mr. Miyamoto accept this award at the 30th anniversary of the D.I.C.E. Awards."

I mean, really, who else could it have been? While the games industry has been built on the backs of millions of people over the years, it's hard to argue that anyone has had a singular impact more than Miyamoto… creating Mario alone would've guaranteed that. That's why it was also no surprise when just last month he became the first game developer to receive the Japanese Order of Culture in its almost 90-year history.

The real question is who will be receiving the award in 10 years' time. Miyamoto was an obvious first choice, but in at the 40th D.I.C.E awards, the likes of Hideo Kojima, Yoko Shimomura, Eiji Aonuma, Alexey Pajitnov, Roberta and Ken Williams, and a ton of other names who would be shoo-ins for an award like this.

#3938. BioWare are gone, but at least you'll be able to watch their final days in a documentary next year and oh wait that's really sad actually

It feels like every single week for the past few years has been the infinitely quotable 30 Rock quote on repeat. That feeling struck particularly last month when EA decided to shut down the iconic Mass Effect and Dragon Age developer BioWare. That obviously resulted in the cancellation of Mass Effect 5, of which a leaked trailer and some, now former, devs made sound pretty interesting. But hey! At least there's a documentary coming next year all about the studio that managed to capture the studio's last days! Yeah, I'm not so convinced by this upside either.

As reported by Deadline, Shane Fennessey and Adam Scorgie will be helming a documentary about the beloved RPG studio for Canada's Super Channel. It's called, punnily enough, Massive Effect: The BioWare Story, and will apparently take a look at its origins in 1995 all the way up to its closure and a bit beyond, planned for release in 2027. Filming began two years ago, so clearly this was meant to be much more of a celebratory project than the funeral procession it's going to be.

Some big names from BioWare's history will be appearing in the doc, including its founders Ray Muzyka, Greg Zeschuk and Augustine Yip, alongside the likes of longtime devs like Mark Darrah, David Gaider, Drew Karpyshyn, Aaryn Flynn, Mac Walters, Trent Oster, James Ohlen and Caroline Livingstone. You can also expect appearances from Jennifer Hale, Casey Hudson and, as if his sole goal is to haunt this industry everywhere, Geoff Keighley.

In a statement, co-founders Muzyka and Zeschuk said, "When the production team asked for our blessing to tell the BioWare story, we were honored and deeply moved. BioWare was never just about the logo or the building. It was about the stories brought to life by the amazing people on our dev teams, and the fans who defended those worlds, championed them and carried them forward. We’re proud this film honors those who made it all possible. The best stories never really end. They live on in our memories and wait for someone to pick them up again."

Obviously the documentary won't only be about the studio's closure, it sounds like a much bigger effort than that, so hopefully it will be a way to recognise how much of an influence BioWare has had on RPGs. It's just a ridiculous shame that it's something of a posthumous release. Continued solidarity with all those at BioWare.

#3935. Take on a time-manipulating corporation in the very Soul Eater meets Jet Set Radio action roguelite CHRONO PUNK

Plus a little bit of Spider-Man, Devil May Cry and Kingdom Hearts

My favourite kind of game that's obviously going for the vibe of a particular era of gaming is one that doesn't look like it's trying to be any other game from said era, moreso if someone told me it was a PS2 or a Dreamcast game everyone forgot about I'd believe you. CHRONO PUNK fits that vibe quite well, an action roguelite that looks like it's taking some cues from those aforementioned consoles, alongside the likes of Soul Eater, Jet Set Radio, Devil May Cry, and Spider-Man.

That is, obviously, a lot of things, but CHRONO PUNK on the surface appears to have its own identity at least. Your player character looks like an almost nightcore version of Sora Kingdom Hearts, with various roles and weapons to choose from; there's a sword and shield, pistols, shurikon, grimoire, and most Soul Eatery of all, a scythe. CHRONO PUNK's got vibes, too. The cities you do combat in are big and nondescript when it comes to details, but ripe for jetting about and Spider-Man-style swinging across the place. And besides, it looks like there's some hub areas ripped straight out of any stylised MMO from the 2000s.

I'm liking the look of the combat too. This'll obviously be one for the combo pilled out there, people who like to bounce back and forth between their enemies like a pinball. Slow paced, this is not. Sick, I hope this is. Pair all of that with some bouncy, wall running movement, and there's some real potential for a strong game here. Sounds like you'll be able to play it in co-op or solo too, which is a nice touch.

The story doesn't seem all that complicated, with some mega corporation manipulating time thereby controlling the city and the masses, leaving you to deal with the mess, but hey, I'm here for the vibes. As of right now, there's no release date attached to CHRONO PUNK, but you can wishlist it on Steam while you wait.

"People realized how easy it was to just share the screen over a Zoom call and everyone's playing."

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

It's no secret that the Covid-19 pandemic saw a lot of people using videogames to stave off lockdown blues, and the Jackbox Party Pack games were especially well-suited for the role: easy-to-understand party fare that's optionally family-friendly and easy to play over a video call. PC Gamer said as much back in March 2020.

In a recent interview with PC Gamer associate editor Ted Litchfield, Jackbox Games CEO Mike Bilder said that the pandemic proved transformative for the developer.

"The industry at large obviously saw a lot of success at that time, but we did as well, and we went from a gamer name to a household name," he said, noting it was an "unfortunate period of time for the world, but for the gaming industry, a good one, and for Jackbox, a good one as well."

"That was kind of a leveling up for Jackbox as a company," said Bilder. "Suddenly office workers are doing happy hours and families over weekends are connecting over a game of Quiplash or something because it's what you did when you were locked down. People realized how easy it was to just share the screen over a Zoom call and everyone's playing."

It surprised employees at the studio to see how popular the games had become.

Chief marketing officer Brooke Hofer recalled a scene in the 2022 Knives Out sequel Glass Onion, where characters could be seen playing Quiplash over a Zoom call: "I remember when we all saw that in the studio, and we're like, 'Whoa,' you know. But that was so many people's experience at that time, and it was cool how that was captured in pop culture in various ways."

#3933. The Game Awards Reveals Its Six Nominees For Game Of The Year, Including GTA 6

With The Game Awards fast approaching on December 10th, the official nominees have been announced today for every single category, including for the big Game of the Year award that takes the main spotlight.

The headline news is that GTA 6 is in the running for that award, even though it hasn't released yet. Nominees for The Game Awards are selected by "a voting jury of over 100 leading media and influencer outlets across the globe", so clearly they think it's worth being in the discussion for GOTY. To be fair, it's a probably a no-brainer.

Here's the full list of nominees for Game of the Year at The Game Awards 2026:

Elsewhere, GTA 6 is in the running for multiple other awards on December 10th, including Best Performance, Best Narrative, Best Action Adventure Game, Best Score & Music and Best Audio Design. It was even revealed in the nominees that Manni L Perez is part of the cast for GTA 6, which hadn't been confirmed until today.

As for Xbox's first-party studios, Fable is up for Most Anticipated Game, Fallout is up for Best Adaptation, Minecraft is up for Best User Creation, Forza Horizon 6 is up for Innovation in Accessibility and Best Sports/Racing Game, Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 and Gears of War: E-Day are up for Best Multiplayer Game, and Gears of War: E-Day is also up for Best Action Game and Innovation in Accessibility.

You can check out the full video where Geoff Keighley runs through each nominee for all the awards down below, and rest assured we'll have complete coverage of the event on December 10th, with plenty of surprises expected for it!

#3932. After taking over EA, Saudi Arabia and their private equity cronies have reportedly held talks about buying Unity

The engine builders have, it's claimed, been working with an investment ​bank to evaluate [their] options

Members of the consortium led by the Saudi Arabian government's Public Investment Fund and some private equity suits which took over EA this year in a leveraged buyout worth $55 billion reportedly have a new target in their sights. Unity, software company and makers of the game engine bearing the same name, have held talks with the consortium over a potential takeover, it's claimed.

According to Reuters, a consortium including Saudi Arabia’s sovereign wealth fund and private equity firm Silver Lake Partners recently approached Unity about a deal that would value the company at around $25 billion. Unity are, it's claimed, currently working with an investment bank to evaluate their options following the chat, with no deal set in stone right now.

Silver Lake, Reuters note, are already among Unity's largest shareholders and invested up to $400 million in the engine builders in 2017. In fact, Silver Lake's managing director and CEO Egon Durban already has a seat on Unity's board of directors, so will probably have to butt out of any takeover talks.

Assuming the consortium would go the leveraged buyout route, loading Unity up with debt like the EA takeover did, it's hard to see any deal not resulting in similarly catastrophic consequences for those working at Unity. EA laid off a reported 400 people in an effort to cut costs after coming under the boot of the Saudi state and private equity, shutting BioWare and cancelling something Sims-related codenamed Project Lotus. BioWare's demise has since been reported to have largely come down to EA execs not wanting to fund both Star Wars Battlefront 3 and Mass Effect 5, with them opting to back only Battlefront 3.

Unity's recent financial results are looking strong, propped up by year-on-year growth in an AI-powered ad network dubbed Vector, so one would assume that bit of the business likely wouldn't be top of the list if any bloodletting was to end up happening.

Solidarity to any Unity workers who're now having to live under the shadow of this prospective takeover and the upheaval it could lead to if it goes ahead in a fashion which mirrors the EA deal.

#3931. 'We Don't Take Your Support for Granted': MLB The Show 27 Revealed for PS5 After Tough Year

Tech Test to return for first time in years

The lifecycle of sports games is always challenging, but I do feel like as MLB The Show has snowballed in popularity it’s lost a lot of its lustre.

San Diego Studio’s plucky baseball sim was once seen as the best sports game on the market, especially compared to stagnant series like Madden NFL and EA Sports FC.

But its industry leading presentation has fallen far behind the curve, and its emphasis on microtransactions in Diamond Dynasty has only increased.

MLB The Show 26 also had its fair share of gameplay flaws, with many criticising the hitting and pitching meta and its netcode.

Today’s aggressively early MLB The Show 27 announcement reads a bit like an apology, then.

In it, bigwig Ramone Russell writes: “We don’t take your time, trust, or support for granted, and we’re incredibly fortunate to have a community that cares so deeply about the game.”

The big takeaway – and the reason for the announcement this early – is that it’s bringing back its Tech Test beta programme.

This hasn’t been a thing since MLB The Show 23, and Russell explains why:

“Game development is challenging, and each year brings its own set of difficult decisions and competing priorities. Some of those decisions resulted in us not holding Tech Tests for the past few years. We appreciate your patience, passion, and continued support, and we’re looking forward to having you be part of the process again. We will provide more details on the Tech Test in the new year.”

So it sounds like San Diego Studio is looking to pool feedback earlier to avoid some of the issues that plagued MLB The Show 26.

It’s also hoping to retain active users by reviving ‘Now & Later’ packs in the current game.

Basically, every pack you buy in Diamond Dynasty now will unlock a pack in MLB The Show 27 next year, encouraging you to engage with this year’s game ahead of the latest release.

To be fair, despite these criticisms, MLB The Show 26 has been a big seller.

As of October, it was the fourth best-selling game of the year in the United States, according to Circana data. It will certainly drop a few places with the release of GTA 6 and The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time, but it should still hold a place in the top ten once the year is done.

There’s no other information about MLB The Show 27 just yet; I imagine that information will follow once the abovementioned Tech Test gets underway.

In an old interview with BBC News back in 2010, which the publication reposted following the casting news, Pattinson expressed his reservations. "I don't know, that's quite big shoes to fill," he said, when asked if it was a role he wanted in the future.

When asked how good a Bond he'd be, he responded: "If I did it right now, probably pretty bad. Pretty embarrassing."

Luckily, Pattinson has had plenty of time since that interview to hone his Bond skills in films like Christopher Nolan's Tenet, Matt Reeves's The Batman, and soon Denis Villeneuve's Dune 3.

Pattinson is picking up the license to kill from Daniel Craig, who played the legendary spy up until 2021's No Time to Die. The news broke after weeks of heavy rumor and speculation about screen tests and the other actors in the running: Josh O'Connor, Callum Turner, Jack Lowden, and Nicholas Hoult. Villeneuve will helm the new film.

"I am overjoyed to welcome Robert Pattinson as our new James Bond. He has the timeless soul of 007 and brings a spirit that is completely new. I cannot wait to begin," Villeneuve said in a press release about the casting.

So far, there's no word on what Bond 26 might be about, and no further casting has been confirmed yet.

#3929. "It's a brave new world": GTA 6's PC port will release sooner than you think to avoid losing money to AI rip-offs, says former Rockstar tech director

"If it's GTA, I think people are gonna try it."

GTA 6's PC release may come sooner than anticipated, according to former Rockstar North technical director Obbe Vermeij, because Rockstar and publishers Take-Two will be concerned about losing money to unofficial generative AI clones of the PS5 version, once it launches on 19th November. In general, Vermeij thinks that how to avoid having your games duplicated by chatbot herders is "the big question" right now for devs and publishers, particularly those who don't have the means to enforce their intellectual property dominions as vehemently as Take-Two do for Grand Theft Auto.

Speaking to me during a wide-ranging chatathon, Vermeij reflected on the early days of Grand Theft Auto development at Rockstar North in the 90s, and how the Noel-and-Liam-Gallagher-esque relationship between PC and console gaming has evolved. He shared a sweary anecdote about the company's difficulties getting the original GTA 1 to look the business on Sony's PlayStation.

"I didn't work on GTA 1 and 2, but I worked for the company at the time, and I was actually right next to the GTA 1 team, so I was able to follow it," he said. "So they worked on PC and then an external company in Dundee did the PlayStation version. Which was really weird, because like, PCs were so much more powerful - still the case, but in those days, it was even more so.

"And I remember, at the time, the GTA team was definitely the most rowdy of all of the teams," Vermeij continued. "And there was one particular day where they sent the PC build away, and then it came back from the PlayStation people, and they had cut down all the textures from 256 colours to 16 colours, and my god, the artist was just going around and swearing - 'what the fuck did they do to our textures, I can't believe it, we can't release this shite'. So it always has been that sort of awkward relationship between PC and the console. So in those days, it was like PC first and then console second, even though that didn't really make much sense for the sales, because the PlayStation versions sold way better."

When it came time to develop GTA 3, Rockstar "flipped that around", Vermeij went on, creating the console versions first. "Clearly the PC market has sort of grown, caught up with the console market, but there's still that same mindset," he said. Most publishers prefer to release all versions at once, Vermeij added, "because then there's only one marketing campaign they have to pay for." GTA lives by its own rules, however. "I guess it's less of an argument for them because the game is just so big, so they just kind of always left it that way. And for developers, it's way easier to just do one version at a time. So, you know, that makes sense."

The arrival of generative AI threatens to throw all this to the winds. Tools such as Reverse Engineer Anything allow for speedy unofficial ports or "slopcomps" of console games on PC, despite warnings from seasoned recomp developers that using genAI for this purpose wrecks the community aspect of unofficial porting, and results in illegible "bruteforce" code rather than preserving some understanding of how the original game was made.

"It really has changed the world," Vermeij observed, "and I think I would be concerned, if I was Rockstar, that somebody would just take the PS5 version and get AI to change it to PC, which won't be won't be as good as their effort, but it could still also hurt their sales. So, I wouldn't be surprised if there was an effort to get [the releases] a little bit closer together. Obviously, I don't really know what they're thinking."

GTA 6 is, according to Rockstar and Take-Two at least, an enormously fiddly production, costing hundreds of millions of dollars over eight years in development. Nonetheless, Vermeij thinks current genAI tools are "probably" capable of pulling off a port. "It will take a long time. It actually, physically takes hours and hours and hours to do these things. And it will take a bunch of tokens and everything, so it would probably cost like, tens of thousands of dollars in tokens. But like, you know, if it's GTA, I think people are gonna try it."

There are already signs that genAI PC port goldrushers are ready to pounce on GTA 6. Just today, Ars Technica reported on efforts to yassify the game's PS5 trailer footage by piping it through a stronker PC graphics card and using Nvidia's DLSS 5 to apply extra layers of gloss.

Vermeij himself left Rockstar way back in 2009 and is now an indie developer. His current early access project is Plentiful, a hexagonal god sim with an emphasis on water physics. It uses "AI-assisted machine translation for localization", but not for "gameplay content, art, or audio". Vermeij is, in general, interested in generative AI despite the surging tide of slopcomp ports. Smaller indie developers are, of course, more vulnerable to the financial fallout from having their work unofficially cloned by generative AI, but Vermeij thinks it's an existential worry for megacorps like Take-Two as well.

"I don't really see how you could protect against that, to be honest," he told me in closing. "I don't see it. But a big company like Take-Two, they would be able to get the lawyers on the case, and maybe, like, you said, for a big game, maybe the AI doesn't really do a particularly good job. But yeah, I mean, it's a brave new world. What was the case before, is that there's so much effort in developing the game, that it is not possible to rip it off, and that's completely changed now. So, yeah, we're going to have to see in the next couple of years, how that's going to pan out."

The latest rumour-mongering places GTA 6's PC release sometime in early 2027. In other news, Rockstar staff are soon to formally vote on whether to apply for union recognition. If the organisers carry the day, the resulting union could encompass nearly all the company's UK staff below management level.

We've already talked a little bit about the New Zealand trick and how it's pretty much the number one topic on social media when it comes to Xbox and GTA 6 right now, so it's naive to think nobody's going to try it this Wednesday.

If you're not in the loop, this refers to people changing their region on Xbox to access GTA 6 at local midnight time in New Zealand, which equates to 6am EST / 11am GMT on Wednesday, November 18th.

News Here's What Xbox Owners Need To Know About 'Moving To New Zealand' For GTA 6

Over the past couple of days, there's been a ton of debate online about whether it's "OK" or "safe" to switch regions in order to play GTA 6 early on Xbox Series X and Xbox Series S, and if you listen to what the majority say, the answer is that Xbox "don't care" if you do it, and that it's happened on many occasions without bans in the past.

However, it's true that Xbox specifically states in its TOCs that you shouldn't change regions unless you've actually moved to the country in question, and over on X/Twitter today, Windows Central editor Jez Corden and YouTuber Colt Eastwood revealed that they talked about this exact topic during a recent visit to Xbox's headquarters in Seattle.

Here's what they had to say about it in response to another of WC's writers (apologies for the profanity in the tweet!):

A lot of people still believe that the risk is extremely low though, with some even arguing that it's "fear mongering" to suggest that Xbox will start suspending or banning people for wanting to play GTA 6 a few hours early.

There are others in the industry, such as The Verge editor Tom Warren, who also believe it's a non-issue:

The reality is that nobody knows for sure whether Xbox will take action against people switching their consoles to New Zealand to play GTA 6 early this Wednesday, but based on historical evidence, it seems pretty unlikely.

#3926. PS5 Does Not Have a 'Monopoly' on Digital Games as £2 Billion Lawsuit Falls Through

Do you remember a few years back when news broke of a potential class action lawsuit against Sony? The case was reported to be worth billions of pounds, which would be dished out as compensation to over 12 million PlayStation users.

Consumer rights campaigner Alex Neill argued that the PlayStation maker had — and continues to have — a monopoly on digital game (and associated DLC) purchases through the PS Store.

Essentially, Neill claimed that Sony was getting away with being able to charge whatever it wanted because of its position as market leader — and consumers were being squeezed dry as a result.

The case really gained traction in 2023 when it was given the greenlight by the UK's Competition Appeal Tribunal, allowing the whole thing to go to trial.

Well, here we are three years later, and Neill's case has ultimately been shot down.

On the 17th November 2026 (that's today, at the time of writing), the aforementioned Tribunal has ruled that the case doesn't prove that Sony has broken the country's competition law. Neill's case has been completely dismissed as a result, although this decision can still be appealed.

The Tribunal also didn't find Sony's pricing to be "excessive and unfair", as per Consumer Voice's report.

This entire case has obviously been given a fresh angle, what with Sony declaring its intentions to stop manufacturing physical game discs in 2028 — a move that will force users to spend money through its digital storefront.

As of right now, though, "the team bringing the claim is considering its options" in regards to appealing the decision.

I'd be surprised if anything more comes of this, however; my understanding is that a totally new case would have to be put forward in order to bring the physical media stuff into the equation.

Did you think this lawsuit would go anywhere? Did you agree with its initial argument? Open up your wallet in the comments section below.

The judgment is rather more nuanced than the headline suggests.

The Tribunal did not find that Sony lacks exclusive control over digital sales on PlayStation. It expressly accepted that digital PlayStation content can only be obtained through the PS Store and that Sony completely controls the digital retail function. If the market could be narrowly defined as "PlayStation digital games" then the Claimant would probably have won.

The case principally failed because the claimant did not establish that “digital PlayStation games” was the correct legal market. The Tribunal found that physical PlayStation games were likely substitutes and that multi-homing (having more than one platform at home), cross-commerce and competition between console systems also constrained Sony. It therefore considered a wider systems market more appropriate. Since the claimant had not advanced an abuse case on that wider market, the case necessarily failed.

Nor did the Tribunal simply find that PlayStation prices are fair, per se. It found that excessive and unfair pricing had not been proved. The claimant’s case depended on an unreliable digital-versus-physical price comparison, and the profitability analysis did not properly account for the way game revenues cross-subsidise console hardware or for relevant intangible assets (e.g. brand goodwill, PSN and PS Store infrastructure).

So the accurate summary is not “Sony does not have a monopoly because Xbox, Nintendo and Steam exist”. It is that the claimant failed to prove the narrower market, dominance and abuse required by competition law.

"We want League to stand the test of time."

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Riot has announced a League of Legends overhaul that promises to touch every aspect of the game.

"We want League to stand the test of time and be a game that's here for many years to come," said League Studio head Andrei "Meddler" van Roon in a teaser trailer. "And there are a lot of things that need to be true to make that happen."

The headlining changes coming with the update, called New Dawn, are a "modernized" client, a graphical revamp for the 5v5 map Summoner's Rift (the last time this happened was in 2014), and "new ways to play" each champion.

While details are scarce in the teaser, some brief footage is shown where you can see what he's talking about: a Blitzcrank player selects what looks like a character-specific mastery tree labeled "God Hand," and it cuts to him beating up an enemy in melee. Other champions are shown using abilities in ways they currently can't—Vayne, for instance, dashes through a wall.

An updated art style is also shown off, including new character models for all sorts of champions as well as bosses like Baron Nashor and the Elder Dragon. It looks much more in line with the art style of Wild Rift, League of Legends' mobile port-slash-spinoff with high-detail character models.

Player reactions are, as you might expect with an update that promises to be so comprehensive, all over the map.

"Am I the only one who thinks this looks like a mobile game," said Reddit user lukesherboiii in a thread sharing the trailer.

#3923. Airframe Ultra's PS1 cyberpunk city is an amazing tribute to G-Police and WipEout, and I wish you people would slow down to appreciate it

But what if we could gawk at the dumpsters

I do not wish to "rule the streets" of Megacity West, dear creators of Airframe Ultra. I wish to be ravished by them, rubbing my face against the rusty corrugated metal of the shipping containers, and savouring the acid blue waters of the bay. I do not want to "become the one thing with freedom in a city of billions: A racer." I want to become the other thing with freedom in a city of billions: a person who slowly drives or – whisper it - walks around just looking at stuff, because gadzooks, this is one of the prettiest PS1 cyberpunk burgs I've laid eyes on.

Those eroded pastel chevrons. Those seductively wobbling vertices. That electric reef of a downtown backdrop, murderously luring your gaze from the on-coming trucks. That layer of invigorating crackle over everything. Every moment or so, I dismount from my hoverbike to inspect some concrete ruin I could swear I last saw in G-Police, or ponder the resemblance between a subway tunnel and WipEout 2097's Gare d'Europa. Then, somebody waps me in the skull with a stop sign at 300 kilometres an hour. But I was already stopped, frantic stranger! Your brutal poetic ironies are wasted on me.

Despite my best efforts, Airframe Ultra is a battle racer. It's co-developed by Videocult, the people behind Rain World – a game it looks nothing like, but is comparable to in the sense that there is an ocean of industrial refuse to navigate, and you will very often die. Each battle race is broken into sprints around a branching course that has been smashed together by the forces of urban decay. You will corkscrew down storm drains and barge through old abandoned clifftop mansions under a scarlet sun, zip along deadly flyovers and thread the barely legible layouts of high density slums.

Your hoverbike handles like a bronco full of helium, and that's before you start wanging it off the gloriously marbled, low-poly rubbish heaps that stud the city, shunting the game's camera through surfaces and exposing the map's underside in what the absolute squares amongst my readers will doubtless deem "an inelegance", but which true turbojunkeys will appreciate for its makeshift exuberance.

You've got a boost button which generally gets you exploded – and all that's before you get to the time-limited battle arenas that bookend each sprint. Here, players attempt to slaughter each other as much as possible, spending collectible cash on floating weapon pick-ups that range from bent pipes to Gatling guns and EMP grenades. Then it's off for another sprint. The first player to earn 10 points and place first in a subsequent sprint wins the match. I have not won many matches. My primary goal right now in Airframe Ultra is persuading everybody to stop and swap some emotes, while I coo over an amazing piece of graffiti I've found.

My efforts to make Airframe Ultra a walking sim aren't just about scenery. The game is surprisingly engrossing on foot, with some woozy tank controls that make me think of the experimental days before every third-person control scheme became a variation on Assassin's Creed, Uncharted or Gears of War. You have to hammer a button to run, for instance, and you'll wind yourself fast. You can also perform punches and kicks in four directions, with grander attacks to discover by smooshing together inputs. You'd best believe I burst into tears when I realised what this reminded me of: it's Bungie's Oni! The game with the finest martial arts system ever coded! There are more obvious influences, like Road Rash, but in these grim days of endless parrying, I'll take all the Konoko callbacks I can get.

Ahhhhh. But if only this had a proper single player mode. Online and local splitscreen with drop-in bot support are all you get. I wouldn't say Airframe is the most balanced deathracer, either. In my experience, and do bear in mind I mostly try to avoid the racing component, victory typically goes to whoever lands a fat cash reserve and grabs an AK47. That mild shambolicness is arguably part of the charm, in that it supplies incentive to stop and drink in the atmosphere. These streets are big and broken and beautiful enough for all of us, friends. Let us rule them together. Read more on Steam.

#3922. Terrific fantasy RPG Queen's Domain gets first proper update, adding a new throwing weapon and options to make puzzles "less frustrating"

Extremely good King's Field-style RPG Queen's Domain – or is it a Metroid Prime homage? Or a stealth Morrowind-up? We hacks simply cannot decide – has received its first proper patch, adding a hitherto "missing" throwing weapon, the Grave Knife, alongside a bunch of quality-of-life fixes.

They've stirred in the ability to disable screenshake, alongside some new icons to make status effects more obvious. They've also introduced "options to make some late game puzzles less frustrating", though they don't specify which. How frustrating! Still, it's a tidy overhaul for a game that has rapidly become one of my 2026 favourites.

The big mystery with the update is what the new Grave Knife does. You'll find it inside the Tower of Knowledge, once you've managed to unlock passage. As for those overly aggravating late game puzzles – I find the toughest part of puzzling in Queen's Domain is often just spotting switches and key objects, so perhaps it's something to do with that?

True, there's a large selection of skeleton tableaus who comically point the way to your next objectives, but the game's pixel aesthetics can be rather dense. I very much approve of this on the whole. I like how organic and tumbledown the environment feels - the repeated delight of realising that, yes, you can get over there, and wow, there's a whole other level down here.

Queen's Domain has earned a lot of happy reactions, and is a solid commercial hit. Developers Freshly Baked say it has sold over 100,000 copies, with Vertical Slice reporting that they've already broken even. Glad tidings indeed. Find the full patch notes below, via Steam.

#3921. Sea of Thieves Nearly Halves Install Size in Latest Update on PS5

Developer Rare is preparing its next major update for its nautical multiplayer adventure, Sea of Thieves, and it makes a pretty big change to the game's storage footprint.

The update, which arrives this week on Thursday 19th November, makes a significant reduction to the title's install size across all platforms.

On PS5, it's moving from about 102.7 GB to a much more palatable 57.4 GB — roughly a 45% decrease.

When the update goes live, you'll need to redownload and install the game, but at its smaller size, so it hopefully won't take you too long.

That's not the only thing coming in the update, of course; the video above goes through numerous additions, like new cosmetics, shanties, December events, and various improvements and fixes.

The timing of the update is almost certainly a coincidence, but if Sea of Thieves has been eating up SSD space on your PS5, the reduction should make installing GTA 6 — a 212 GB monster — a bit easier.

Are you still enjoying Sea of Thieves on PS5? Tell us in the comments section below.

#3920. I just found out you can use your Steam Wishlist to search for deals on games outside of Steam, saving my nephew more than £40 on Total War: Warhammer 3

It earned me a bucketload of uncle points

I may be very late to the party with this discovery, but I only just realised you can connect your Steam Wishlist to a third-party deals tracker. The beauty of which is that, once hooked up, you can see what games you've been pining for are going cheap not just on Steam but through any major shopfront across the internet.

I worry that I will be coming across as 'Use this one trick to save money – greengrocers hate it!', but it's already helped save my nephew more than £40. Even if it meant using a slightly underhand method.

Two weeks ago, I got a text from my nephew asking what the best way to play Total War: Warhammer 3. When I messaged back a couple of hours later (look, I'm not a responsive uncle) to tell him it's currently £50 on Steam, but it's worth waiting because according to SteamDB's price history it's come down to £7.50 in the past, I was too late. He'd got itchy feet and bought it at full whack on Steam, using up all his birthday money.

That's when I went looking and found Is There Any Deal for the first time. (A lot of you in the comments may be throwing your hands up in despair to hear this oversight) If you've not come across it before, it's a site that tracks game sales across loads of shops, including Steam, EA Store, Epic Games Store, GamersGate, GOG. GreenManGaming, Humble. This means while a game may not be on sale on Steam you can see if it's on sale anywhere else.

In the case of Total War: Warhammer 3, while it was full price on Steam, over on the Humble Store it was discounted to £7.49. I sent a link to my nephew and then told him, using the authority only an uncle has, that it's okay to refund the game through Steam and buy the cheaper version. It's not something I've ever done myself, but he's 17 and that is a lot of money to save.

Anyway, that's recommendation the first. It was only when I was looking for a way to export my Steam Wishlist to ask RPS supporters what I should cull that I realised Is There Any Deal has another feature: you can import every game on your Wishlist to get deal notifications. (This may get a second groan of despair in the comment section.) Once linked up, the site will ping you a notification whenever games you're waiting for pop up in a deal.

Just looking at my current list, I can get Genesis Noir, Ancient Enemy, and Norco for £10 total, all of which with more than 70% discounts through stores other than Steam. So, as you can see, this could be both a saving technically and lead me to spending a lot more money than I mean to…

You may already have heard of these tools, but as I hadn't I thought it best to give them a shout out.

Now considering I've revealed myself to be a rube, what other third party tools should I be installing to weaponise my Steam Library?

It's estimated that almost 15 million copies of GTA 6 have been sold

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

GTA 6 isn't even out yet, but it's been estimated that Rockstar's next game has already surpassed $1.45 billion in revenue, with almost 15 million copies sold via pre-orders.

That's according to market intelligence firm Sensor Tower, whose latest sales tracker estimates – updated yesterday – continue to put PS5 pre-orders well ahead of Xbox Series X|S, with sales for Sony's console thought to account for 74% of the lot, at 11.13 million copies. Between both platforms, Sensor Tower estimates 14.94 million units have been sold.

What's more, as of November 10, Sensor Tower estimated that a whopping 87% of all GTA 6 pre-orders were for the more expensive Ultimate Edition. As a reminder of the different GTA 6 versions, the Standard Edition is $80, while the Ultimate Edition comes in at $100, the price everyone was so worried about before pre-orders were announced. For your extra $20, you get some unique cars and several exclusive shops, among other things – I imagine those shops may have been the selling point for many, given that you're literally missing out on content otherwise.

To an extent, I'd imagine a bit of a 'go big or go home' mindset might apply here, too. After all, we've been waiting 13 years since the last game in the series, so a lot of people are just going to want the, well, ultimate experience. It's this sort of thinking that could get you to spend $400 on a box of mostly expensive tat, though, so be careful with that.

Anyway, there was never any doubt GTA 6 sales would be massive, but it'll be interesting to see exactly where they land at and after launch. Sony and Microsoft have already announced that it's the most pre-ordered game of all time on their respective digital storefronts, and there are still a couple of days to go until release. According to Sensor Tower, though, the biggest spike in pre-orders came right after the release of Netflix's Extended Look – sales rose 6x compared to the previous tracked day, with August 28 (the day after the premiere) thought to have brought in around $16.3 million in revenue. So, it sounds like most people were already sold once they got a proper look at the gameplay footage.

GTA 6 preloads are already live, so if you've pre-ordered the digital version – or the code-in-a-box release, if you have yours – you can start getting it downloaded now so you're ready for launch on November 19.

While you're here, be sure to check in on our GTA 6 countdown. If you're getting ready for release day, you can also look at our recommendations for the best controllers and headsets to play GTA 6.

#3918. Real-time strategy game The Fertile Crescent 2 is an isometric odyssey inspired by Age of Empires, with the 1.0 release out now

Time to power-rank the biggest Bronze Age civs

Age of Empires-influenced real-time strategy game The Fertile Crescent 2: Collapse of the Bronze Age leaves early access today, publishers MicroProse have announced, with the 1.0 version adding the final chapters of the singleplayer story. You'll also get your grubby fingers on the very same map editor developers Wield Interactive used to design the campaign.

I'm new to The Fertile Crescent 2 myself. I do like the sound of a strategy sim in which you guide a fugitive community through the Late Bronze Age Collapse. The land has been thrown into turmoil by the arrival of the Sea People, this being a loose historical term for assorted ocean-going migrants who, I gather, are often blamed for the crumbling of the Hittites among other once-glorious Bronze Age powers. I don't have much scholarly insight to share - I thought the "Sea People" referred to expansionist mermaids, at first - but I do have a trailer.

Nate Crowley (RPS in peace) was exceedingly fond of the original game, calling it "a bite-sized chunk of phenomenal RTS design" that "manages to riff nostalgically on Age Of Empires, while completely rewriting its ground rules". The sequel continues with the same core concepts – above all, the paramount importance of food, which determines population and army size together with your civ's progression.

"This is not a game about building the biggest empire," the developers explain in a press release. "Resources have to be managed, stability is fragile, and growth comes with risk. Every expansion, every battle, and every decision must be weighed against survival. Building and managing a sustainable economy is as important as commanding your forces in battle. Expanding your army too quickly can put your food economy under pressure."

The story spans 17 missions, with four playable factions: the Assyrians, Egyptians, Babylonians, and Hittites. The 1.0 release also includes some standalone scenario missions, a skirmish mode, and multiplayer on dedicated servers with bot support.

Read more on Steam. If you're partial to historical strategy and don't mind winding back the clock (upturning the hourglass? Adjusting the sundial? Recalibrating the henge?) another few thousand years, Folk Emerging is pretty terrific. If you like stories about migrant tribes, and you don't mind trading your Hittites for Vikings, you might get a kick out of The Banner Saga.

When World of Warcraft: Forever's beta first launched, I lamented its long stretches of silence and penchant for ambience over theatrics. I still sort of stand by that, but after spending more time in Azeroth (and discovering the loop music setting) I've a new-found appreciation for both WoW's soundtrack and ambient music as a whole.

It's also got me thinking about what makes a soundtrack ambient versus something more melodic. I'm chronically Final Fantasy 14-brained, where just about everything has a grand thematic soundtrack to it—the jauntiness of the Gold Saucer, the soothing Middle-earthness of Gridania's outer Shroud zones, the grand organs of Ishgard's bitterly cold landscape. You can't escape composer Masayoshi Soken's penchant for leifmotifs. He will turn anything into an orchestral spectacle.

I'm a big JRPG fan in general, a genre I think is the absolute master of thematic soundtracks. But I also think fondly of games I've played over the years that are a little more pared down, their soundtracks there for a little atmosphere rather than actively driving the narrative. Minecraft's OST is a masterclass in ambience, and is in regular rotation across my videogame-themed Spotify playlists. I also have a huge soft spot for the soundtrack behind Mirror's Edge—one which settles in this almost otherworldly ambiance, only ramping up when Faith is in a perilous situation.

But what about you? Do you prefer the more subtle nuances that an atmospheric soundtrack has to offer? Or do you like your videogame music loud, in your face, and full of dramatics? Be sure to leave a comment and let me know which one's your favourite and why.

Exodus has lifted the veil on the female version of its protagonist Jun, via a brand new trailer.

The context around this one is interesting, because developer Archetype Entertainment famously redesigned its male lead just a few weeks back, following on from fan criticism of his original mug.

For what it's worth, the initial reaction to female Jun has been much more positive, with the comments section of the aforementioned trailer housing plenty of praise. Here's hoping that the studio's nailed this one first time!

It's worth pointing out that you can customise Jun's appearance but not to any significant extent. You can edit their hair, facial hair, eye colour, and makeup, can't change their facial structure.

The trailer doesn't start and end with female Jun, however. A feature on Jun's personality and background follows, giving a little more insight into the kind of character you'll be playing as.

To be clear, you'll be able to shape Jun's story through your actions throughout the game. A Mass Effect-style alignment system determines the narrative's direction as you go from mission to mission and get to know your allies.

"They would never stop working on this game if they had the choice"

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Rob Nelson, co-studio head of Rockstar North and GTA 6 lead, has explained that the game took so long simply because the studio had the option to.

I don't think I'm surprising anyone by saying that GTA 6 has taken quite a while to come out. It's been 13 years, two console generations, and four Doctor Who actors since GTA 5, and it's made GTA 6 the most-anticipated game of all-time. And considering the first 10 GTA games were released in just 12 years, it kind of puts things into perspective just how long it's been, which feels even weirder when you realise we're just about a day away before people in New Zealand start playing it.

Speaking to The Guardian, Rockstar Games head of publishing Jennifer Kolbe adds that the devs "would never stop working on this game if they had the choice," with Nelson explaining, "it's really hard to close it down." He adds that with "a little bit of space from it, you can look at it objectively and go: 'I'm proud of what we've done.'" In the end, "it is being taken away from you."

Nelson questions that if a developer had as many resources as Rockstar did, wouldn't they also go for the most ambitious game they could possibly make? He explains, "What we have grappled with is the transition from being limited by technical constraints to being limited by human resource constraints," adding, "You can keep going forever… People say you can throw money at the problem, and you can to an extent, but it's no guarantee of making something good."

Kolbe adds, "They could have made GTA 5.5 and done it faster," but that “ultimately, that's not what they wanted." Nelson chimes in, "You have to take big swings. It can't be just more of the same."

Be sure to take a look at our GTA 6 countdown and our guide to the different GTA 6 versions ahead of launch. Getting ready for release? You can also look at our recommendations for the best controllers and headsets to play GTA 6.

4. Best pro Xbox: Nacon Revolution X Unlimited

#3912. After Star Wars Zero Company dev Bit Reactor brought back an unspecified number of furloughed devs, some of those who weren't have seemingly been laid off

"I’m really proud of what we built together"

Early last month, Star Wars Zero Company developer Bit Reactor brought back a number of developers who had been furloughed before the game launched in August. At the time they did not specify how many devs were returning to the studio, with a separate report claiming more than half had become full time staffers again. Unfortunately, it does now seem like not everyone was able to be brought back, with a number of now former workers sharing word of having been laid off.

As spotted by Star Wars outlet Bespin Bulletin, multiple developers shared word of their layoffs to LinkedIn. A producer at Bit Reactor, Michael Blackard was seemingly one of the first to report being laid off, alongside senior QA analyst Ryan Mosher. Ryan Lopez, an environment artist at the studio, shared, "I was laid off from Bit Reactor this week after a three-month furlough, and while it stings, I’m really proud of what we built together." Lopez had apparently been working on the game for more than three years, starting all the way back on the game's pre-production period.

Tyler Eichten, a UI engineer, also said, "As of today, my time with Bit Reactor has come to a close due to a layoff. I am immensely proud of the work that I, the UI/UX team, and the team at large have accomplished. I hope that in this tumultuous industry that my coworkers (and myself) find placement." It's unclear at this point in time if any, or how many, other staffers have been formally laid off, and Bit Reactor are yet to make a comment.

Star Wars Zero Company performed very well both critically and commercially, making it all the more disappointing that not all of those who worked on the game, who made it as great as it seemingly is, get to continue working at the studio. As always, solidarity with all devs affected.

#3911. The Game Awards 2026 Nominees Revealed, GTA 6 Up for 8 Awards

Full list of The Game Awards 2026 category nominees

Geoff Keighley has today confirmed the nominees for all the categories at The Game Awards 2026, with the show set to take place on 10th December 2026.

The nominees for Game of the Year are: 007 First Light, Control Resonant, GTA 6, Phantom Blade Zero, Resident Evil Requiem, and The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time.

GTA 6 has been nominated the most, in eight categories in total. Its other nominations include Best Game Direction, the Best Narrative, and Best Performance.

Below you'll find all the nominees for every noteworthy category at The Game Awards 2026. I have omitted the e-sports-related awards, but you can find the full list on The Game Awards website.

Hello Bond, goodbye Batman: Due to The Batman 2 delays, Robert Pattinson is no longer obligated to make another Batman movie

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The Batman 2 has taken so long to make that Robert Pattinson is reportedly no longer legally contracted to appear in a third movie, leaving the future of DC Elseworlds' Caped Crusader unclear.

According to a new report from The Wrap, "the protracted production of The Batman: Part II has allowed Pattinson to slip out from under his contract." The deal originally held the star to make a third and final outing as the Gotham vigilante. But now that the contract will have seemingly timed out by the time of a third movie, it is not clear what will happen to Pattinson's Bat.

The Batman sequel has seen its fair share of setbacks. Originally set to release in October 2025, it was pushed back multiple times all the way to early 2028. Most recently, the project was momentarily put on hold when director Matt Reeves stepped away from production for personal reasons. However, filmmaker Steven Soderbergh has now taken the reins. Still, The Batman: Part II is certainly a long time coming, as the first movie hit screens in 2022 – six years before the sequel is set to release.

Pattinson's recent casting as a legendary agent 007 further complicates things. On November 16, it was announced that Pattinson had been cast as the next James Bond, in Amazon MGM Studios' first take on the British spy led by Dune director Denis Villeneuve. Despite Pattinson previously stating he would only sign on to three Bond movies and being a few years older than the other candidates, he still landed the role.

James Bond movies are a huge undertaking, which will certainly take up a lot of Pattinson's time moving forward, leaving little room for The Batman. Alas, Pattinson has proven he can take on big projects one after the other. Just this year, Pattinson has starred in The Drama, The Odyssey, Primetime, and will be introduced to the world of Dune this December in Villeneuve's third and final movie.

There is also the issue of DC Studios. Just last week, it was announced that James Gunn and Peter Safran would be stepping down as DC Studios co-CEOs, and are set to be replaced by former Marvel Studios executive Jeremy Latcham on December 1, 2026. The shakeup arrived not long after Skydance-owned Paramount acquired Warner Bros. Reports suggest that Skydance plans to "dismantle" Gunn's DCU Chapter One.

Though The Batman isn't part of the DCU, the fate of all current DC projects remains ambiguous. DC Studios, Pattinson, and Reeves have yet to comment on the matter.

The Batman 2 is set to hit theaters on February 18, 2028. For more, check out our guide on how to watch the DC movies in order and keep up with other upcoming DC movies and shows.

#3908. "I feel that sense of responsibility more acutely": After BioWare's closure, the makers of a new Mass Effect 3 co-op remaster mod look to carry their legacy

"It's like watching a friend lose a parent - maybe you're not attached, but you feel the secondhand distress"

It appears I was premature in suggesting that the closure of BioWare might quickly spell an end for Mass Effect 3's strangely good, preposterously enduring co-op mode. I reinstalled and logged on just last week, and easily found a series of packed lobbies. Still, it was always regrettable that 2021's Mass Effect Legendary Edition opted not to remaster this multiplayer component alongside its dolled-up main trilogy, thus failing to introduce to a new generation the joys of performing teleporting psychic headbutts as a millennia-old bipedal frog.

This oversight has now been addressed, with the release of the Legendary Edition Multiplayer mod for said remaster. It's both a reconstruction and a slight expansion of ME3 multi, built in secret since 2023 by the ME3Tweaks group: a modding collective who've previously imbued the Legendary Edition with Mass Effect 1's Pinnacle Station DLC. It's also, some of its makers tell me, a bittersweet expression of appreciation for a series that looks unlikely to continue after EA's Mass Effect 5 cancellation.

At least some of that affection can be seen in how Legendary Edition Multiplayer differs from the already-available LEMP mod, which uses AI vibecoding to slap a mechanically identical recreation of ME3's co-op into the Legendary Edition's ones and zeroes. ME3Tweaks's version instead adds, according to member and longtime ME modder Audemus, a "completely overhauled UI, rebaked level lighting, upscaled and redrawn textures, upgraded shaders, native LE features such as HDR and controller support, networking and server replication improvements, extensive bug fixes, and entirely new wave modes such as Unified and Coalition."

Unified mode, for instance, quite literally mixes up ME3's enemy factions by forming mishmashed waves of baddies from across the Geth, Reaper, and Cerberus armies, thereby dusting off and stamping on your 14-year-old battle tactics. The mod also offers the ability to use ME3Tweaks' own servers for matchmaking, though a private server option remains for scraps with mates.

I'll definitely be giving this a try, once I'm back from my current travels. Though as with those OG ME3 multiplayer sessions last week, it'll be with a certain glumness, knowing that – despite a vocal campaign to give Mass Effect 5 a reprieve– I'll be playing something that had its future cut short.

The circumstances aren't lost on Legendary Edition Multiplayer's creators. "BioWare's closure is an incredibly sad moment for the games industry, and a particularly heartbreaking thing for the Mass Effect fanbase to contend with," Audemus tells me over email. "I feel as though our responsibility as a modding community has always been to carry the torch for this franchise, with or without an official future for it. But now that the future of Mass Effect has never been more in question, I feel that sense of responsibility more acutely than I ever have before."

Mgamerz, another modder on the project, recalls how "The day BioWare closed it didn't hit me until later in the day, a sort of numbness I can't really describe. I've spent 14 years working on their games - it's like watching a friend lose a parent - maybe you're not attached, but you feel the secondhand distress."

For some Legendary Edition Multiplayer modders, the affected BioWare staff included developers they knew personally. ME3Tweaks had previously been invited to embargoed discussions with both BioWare and EA on game modding, and Mass Effect writer and director Mac Walters (who left BioWare voluntarily in 2023) allegedly advocated for an even closer relationship.

"It's a shame to see it shut down," Mgamerz says. "Everyone speculated about it, but I know from talking to people internally there, that nobody knew the guillotine was about to drop." [Owners EA say the decision was only made after "months of planning, review, and analysis", though independent reporting suggests it was largely down to a straight choice between making ME5 or Star Wars Battlefront 3.]

"When we had our NDA with BioWare (since expired), apparently Mac Walters pushed internally to get my dev team brought into the manifold," he adds. "I say this as 'apparently', cause due to scheduling issues we never got to speak with Mac. But secondhand stories tell me he was a big proponent of modders - something that I would have loved to see more publicly shown.

"It is disappointing to know that the people who helped build the world my work now builds upon were killed unceremoniously - a problem that plagues the industry, and what kept me from further pursuing entry into it, something I used to dream of doing when I was younger."

RPS lawyers are telling me to tell you that nobody was literally killed. All the same, and even as someone much more familiar with playing the Mass Effects than tinkering around in their engine bays, the ME3Tweaks team make relatable points: we can frolick around an uprezzed Firebase Hydro, biotically biffing half-robot Turians like it's 2012, but it'll be hard not to look at all those conspicuous waist-high walls and think about the people who put them there. The same's true of having your mind drift to thoughts of their successors.

But there's another way of looking at it, which is that mods like Legendary Edition Multiplayer can preserve and maintain an original developer's work well beyond what their leveraged-buyout executive overlords might deem financially inconvenient. "I hope," as Audemus puts it, "that this mod - along with the fact that we've been able to build the technology to make mods like this in the first place - sends a message that there is incredible value in this franchise, and a passionate fanbase that is not ready to say goodbye to this universe and these games."

#3907. Mercenaries Grace launches November 25 for PS5 in Japan, in December for Switch, and in early 2027 for PC

Strategy RPG Mercenaries Grace will launch for PlayStation 5 on November 25 in Japan for 3,850 yen, followed by Switch in December, and PC via Steam in early 2027, developer RideonJapan announced.

Here is an overview of the game, via its Steam page:

A young mercenary spreads his wings toward tomorrow! A tale of an iron prosthetic and an unwanted queen.

Mercenaries Grace is a tactical simulation RPG set in a fantasy world. Battles occur on quarter-view maps with height differences, where character positioning in the front, back, and side of enemy units may very well determine each battle’s outcome.

The Kingdom of Grauses has long suffered under the tyranny and crushing taxes of the Regent O’Neill. With his sudden death in battle, the citizens rejoiced, expecting the long-awaited coronation of the late king’s heir.

Meanwhile, a small unit attacks the “Forbidden Tower” located in a taboo land in the northern reaches of the kingdom. Among them are the “Iron Hand Mercenaries,” led by the young mercenary Swan—the right-hand man of the legendary iron-prosthetic-wielding leader, Garsh. From the depths of the Forbidden Tower, Swan and his comrades rescue the beautiful General Berta. However, she turns out to be the biological younger sister of the late Regent O’Neill.

Upon her release, Berta is pushed forward by O’Neill’s former loyalists to be crowned as the next queen. What chaos will be unleashed by this unlawful ascension, driven by corrupt ministers desperate to protect their own vested interests? And where will the hands of fate lead Swan and Berta?

Mercenaries Grace is a tactical simulation RPG set in a rich fantasy world.

Battles take place on quarter-view isometric maps with distinct elevation changes. Strategy is paramount: combat outcomes shift based on whether you attack from the front, back, or sides, and positioning allies correctly unlocks powerful support effects.

Use Skill Points earned in battle to learn and upgrade skills, change classes, and enjoy highly customizable character progression.

Featuring stunning character designs by illustrator mitsu_plus! Watch the beautifully drawn characters come to life with a rich array of emotional expressions.

While previous entries in the Mercenaries Saga series utilized a phase-based system where all player characters acted followed by all enemy characters, this title introduces a massive overhaul!

Combat now shifts to an alternate-turn system—similar to chess or shogi—where players and enemies take turns moving one character at a time. Predicting who to move next and anticipating the enemy’s sequence adds a whole new layer of depth to the battlefield.

The “Ladder Class” System: Eight Branching Paths

In previous titles, each character started in an initial class that split into two intermediate paths, eventually leading to advanced and special classes for a total of seven possibilities.

This game introduces the “Ladder Class” system, breaking past traditional boundaries like Warrior, Thief, Priest, and Mage into eight distinct lineages. As characters promote through Novice, Intermediate, Advanced, and Special tiers, they are not locked into a linear path—they can also cross over to adjacent class branches.

How you grow your characters as they climb the ranks is entirely up to you!

Midway through the story, a pivotal choice will cause the narrative to split drastically.

While previous entries changed story developments and recruitable allies based on your route, this game introduces completely unique “Awakening” systems for each path that temporarily power up your units. The “Awakening” command unlocks after progressing past a certain point in the story. Much like the “Soul Exceed” ultimate moves, it is activated by consuming accumulated power stocks.

What kind of power-ups await you on each path? Play and find out!

Engaging in combat fills a gauge in the top right corner of the screen. By consuming stocked power, characters can unleash their ultimate move: “Soul Exceed.”

These ultimate abilities vary by Ladder Class—ranging from dealing devastating damage to enemies to fully healing the party’s HP and removing status ailments.

Mastering these ultimate moves is the ultimate key to victory!

Battlefields are now rendered in full 3D models, allowing players to freely rotate the camera angle during their turn.

Changing your perspective might even reveal hidden items tucked away in the environment!

The options menu includes features perfect for replayability and grinding, such as toggling the 3D battle map grid ON/OFF, streamlining skill animations with “Simple Skill Effects,” and accelerating gameplay with “Fast Movement.”
